verses.1: Al-Mizan reads the definite al- in al-kāfirūn as referring to a known, particular group of disbelievers, not all disbelievers, since the following verses order the Prophet to declare dissociation from their religion and foretell their rejection of his.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the verse begins the script given to the Prophet. Mā refers to the idols they worship. Lā negates the future, unlike mā, which negates the present; he therefore declares that he will never worship the idols they worship now.
verses.3: Al-Mizan takes the future wording as a forecast that these particular disbelievers will never enter the monotheistic religion. Joined to Say (109:1), it means that the Prophet must continue worshipping God forever and foretell that they will never worship Him, so no common religious ground can exist; it parallels (36:7) and (2:6). Mā is used rather than man for parallelism with the preceding verse.
verses.4: Al-Mizan first treats the repetition of the previous two statements as emphasis, like (102:3-4) and (74:19-20). Another reading makes mā maṣdariyyah, turning the clauses to one’s act of worship: the parties have nothing in common either in their object of devotion—God or idols—or their manner of worship, God-ordained or invented through ignorance and false attribution. It therefore makes the repetition substantive, but Al-Mizan judges the reading far from the apparent sense and says the narration discussion supplies another, subtle explanation.

verses.6: Al-Mizan says the lām in lakum and lī expresses ikhtiṣāṣ, exclusive affiliation and possession: their idolatrous religion belongs only to them and excludes the Prophet, while his religion belongs only to him and excludes them. The verse thus reiterates their lack of common ground; it does not permit choosing any religion or mean that the Prophet ceased opposing theirs, which would contradict the Qur’an’s call to truth. Readings of dīn as jazāʾ, or as an omitted “reward of your religion,” are both far from the apparent sense.
